The passage argues that slavery is an underrecognized foundation for understanding pedagogy, especially as digital surveillance expands in education and work. Using Foucault’s theory of panopticism, it examines surveillance as a tool of extraction, capitalist power, and behavioral control. It connects Foucault’s ideas about schools, prisons, discipline, examination, and record keeping to racial surveillance and the history of slavery.

The author reviews pedagogical discourse and notes that many accounts define pedagogy as teaching practice while overlooking its ancient association with enslaved pedagogues in Greece and Rome. The passage contrasts education as more person-centered with pedagogy as often outcome-centered and disciplinary. It also discusses data-driven pedagogy, learning analytics, and digital platforms, arguing that these systems extract and use student data while often lacking transparency.

The passage draws on fugitive pedagogy to describe how African American educators resisted racial surveillance, violence, and restrictions on Black education. It links racial chattel slavery, plantation management, record keeping, torture, and productivity measurement to later forms of scientific management, surveillance capitalism, and school discipline. It also discusses the school-to-prison pipeline as a continuation of carceral practices affecting students of color.

The author introduces “surveillance pedagogy” to describe teaching and learning shaped by monitoring, data extraction, textualization, and behavioral management in formal and informal settings. Digital platforms such as Google Classroom are presented as examples of systems that collect educational data and influence learning processes. The passage concludes that contemporary digital surveillance and surveillance capitalism extend older extractive practices associated with slavery, making slavery central to future discussions of pedagogy.

This cross-sectional study assessed lung function decline and associated factors among heroin users on methadone therapy attending the MAT clinic at Muhimbili National Hospital in Dar-es-salaam, Tanzania. Of 310 enrolled participants, 302 completed questionnaires and spirometry. Participants had a mean age of 42.78 years, 95.7% were male, and 20.9% were underweight. Most were current cigarette smokers (83.8%), and 19.9% had a history of injecting heroin. HIV infection was present in 9.6%, and 32.8% reported a history of pulmonary tuberculosis.

Lung function decline, defined as FEV1 <70%, was found in 28.5% of participants, with a mean age of onset of 44 years. Restrictive lung disease was the most common pattern (13.2%), followed by obstructive lung disease (11%) and mixed abnormality (4.3%). Independent factors associated with lung function decline were being underweight, HIV infection, and history of pulmonary tuberculosis. Underweight participants were 4.7 times more likely to have lung function decline, HIV-positive participants 2.6 times more likely, and those with prior pulmonary tuberculosis 2.4 times more likely.

The study concludes that over a quarter of clients attending the MAT clinic had lung function decline and recommends routine lung function screening to address undiagnosed and underdiagnosed lung diseases in this population.

The Superior Court of Pennsylvania affirmed Clay Williams’s life sentence for first-degree murder and related convictions stemming from the 2005 shooting death of Mizael Velez during an attempted cell phone robbery in a Philadelphia Chinese store. The court denied Williams’s petition to remand for further record development and dismissed his ineffective assistance of counsel claims without prejudice to raise on collateral review. The court found several appellate claims waived, including challenges to suppression, sufficiency of the evidence, and admission of a witness statement, due to inadequate preservation or argument.

The passage introduces BALLAST, a Bayesian active learning method for placing Lagrangian ocean drifters to improve inference of time-dependent ocean currents. It frames drifter deployment as a spatio-temporal active learning problem, where placement locations are selected sequentially to maximize expected information gain about a vector field. The method models ocean currents with a spatio-temporal vector-output Gaussian process using a temporal Helmholtz kernel and noisy velocity observations. BALLAST accounts for Lagrangian observation structure by simulating hypothetical trajectories from surrogate vector fields and uses an information-theoretic utility. The authors also develop a Gaussian process posterior sampling approach combining standard GP regression with the stochastic partial differential equation approach for efficient computation. Numerical results are reported to show benefits for sequential observer deployment on synthetic and high-fidelity ocean current models.

Amazon.com, Inc. filed a Form 8-K reporting that shareholders approved an amendment to its Restated Certificate of Incorporation for a 20-for-1 common stock split and a proportionate increase in authorized common shares. The amendment was filed in Delaware on May 27, 2022; shareholders of record on May 27 were to receive 19 additional shares per share around June 3, with split-adjusted trading expected June 6. A report commissioned by the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario says school fundraising in affluent areas undermines the province’s learning opportunities grant for needy schools. The grant provides about $179 per student, while school-generated funds average $280 per student and total $548 million, nearly $200 million more than the government’s equity-focused funding. Economist Hugh Mackenzie’s report says boards receiving less grant money often raise more, while those receiving more grant support raise less.

The report reviews Ontario’s 1997 education funding formula, saying special education, ESL supports, and school maintenance have been underfunded for two decades. It notes provincial education spending is now $23 billion, or $12,107 per student, with much of the increase going to class-size reductions and full-day kindergarten. ETFO president Sam Hammond said boards still struggle to fund special education, despite recent government changes and an added $219 million for staff.

ETFO is calling for five-year reviews of the funding system, more funding for special education and mental health, and more support staff. School-generated funds are used for enrichment programs, computers, gym equipment, field trips, and other school needs.

The Fifth Circuit affirmed Joe Ezeokeke’s 138-month sentence for possession of cocaine with intent to distribute. The court held that the district court properly applied an obstruction of justice adjustment based on false, material trial testimony adopted through the presentence report. It also found his within-guidelines sentence substantively reasonable and concluded he failed to rebut its presumption of correctness.

A medRxiv preprint analyzed 1,284 participants from the Kailuan cohort to examine links between long-term visit-to-visit blood pressure variability and cerebral small vessel disease (cSVD). Blood pressure variability from 2006–2022 was assessed for systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure, and pulse pressure, while MRI identified cSVD markers including white matter hyperintensities, lacunae, cerebral microbleeds, and visible perivascular spaces.

cSVD was found in 69.3% of participants. Higher systolic blood pressure variability was associated with moderate cSVD burden and visible perivascular spaces. Higher diastolic blood pressure variability was associated with lacunae. Higher pulse pressure variability showed stronger associations with moderate or severe cSVD burden, lacunae, and visible perivascular spaces. Associations varied by age and hypertension status: pulse pressure variability was especially associated with cSVD markers in adults under 60, while systolic and pulse pressure variability effects on cSVD burden were significant mainly among participants with hypertension.

The study concludes that higher long-term blood pressure variability, particularly with hypertension, is an independent risk factor for total cSVD burden, lacunae, and visible perivascular spaces, and that pulse pressure variability may be especially relevant in younger adults.

Gary Gensler’s lecture marks Bitcoin’s 10th anniversary and reviews its growth, including its price, market size, mined coins, transaction volume, hash rate, electricity use, unique addresses, nodes, ICO activity, and volatility. The class discusses whether Bitcoin’s future value or market capitalization will rise, fall, or change through forks or altered monetary policy.

The lecture then examines payment-system pain points: many intermediaries and ledgers, high costs, delayed settlement, limited financial inclusion, cross-border currency conversion, chargebacks, fraud, privacy concerns, cybersecurity risks, and identity theft. Blockchain’s potential benefits are framed around lowering verification and networking costs, but challenges include scalability, slow processing, high transaction costs, interoperability, error resolution, governance, regulation, liquidity, and volatility.

Students debate whether payment finality is desirable, since merchants may want irreversible settlement while consumers may value chargebacks and error correction. Gensler notes that delayed settlement may persist for business reasons, though technology could enable faster settlement in payments and securities.

The class discusses whether blockchain is necessary for smart contracts and payments, or whether it may mainly push existing systems such as Swift, Visa, MasterCard, and banks to improve. A MasterCard employee argues existing systems can provide similar functions and already have acceptance and scale, while others argue blockchain may help underserved regions, censorship resistance, and new programmable-payment use cases. India’s non-blockchain payment innovations are cited as another model for financial inclusion.

Examples of blockchain payment companies include BitPay, Ripple, R3, Quorum, and Bakkt. BitPay lets merchants accept Bitcoin and convert it to fiat for a 1% fee. Gensler describes how the Hillary Clinton campaign considered but rejected accepting Bitcoin donations due to legal and practical concerns. The lecture also mentions philanthropic digital-asset donations and a Media Lab vending machine accepting Bitcoin, Litecoin, and a stablecoin.

For cross-border payments, Gensler explains the correspondent-banking model and the idea of using crypto as a bridge between fiat currencies, as in Ripple’s xRapid. Potential benefits include fewer intermediaries, faster settlement, weekend availability, and lower costs for small remittances, but drawbacks include volatility, liquidity needs, bid-ask spreads, arbitrage limits, and added risk. The lecture concludes by framing future classes around evaluating when blockchain-like systems are useful.

The passage explains Bollinger Bands, a technical indicator with a moving average and upper/lower bands based on standard deviations, and describes using ChatGPT to create and backtest a Bollinger Bands trading strategy in Python. ChatGPT proposed a squeeze strategy where Bollinger Bands move inside Keltner Channels, which use ATR for band calculation. The strategy buys and holds when the lower Bollinger Band is above the lower Keltner band and the upper Bollinger Band is below the upper Keltner band, and sells when either condition fails. Backtested on SPY from 1993 without dividend or split adjustment, the strategy produced low, erratic compounded returns and a drawdown considered too high. The article concludes that while ChatGPT generated and backtested an unusual strategy effectively, the strategy was not profitable enough for live trading.

Geologists from Queensland’s Department of Natural Resources and Mines and the University of Queensland found evidence of platinum, gold and rare earth elements in western Queensland. The area, referred to as the Diamantina Minerals Province, includes rare geological pipe structures south-west of Mount Isa near the Northern Territory border. These pipes may contain minerals including scandium, cobalt, nickel, copper, rare earth elements, silver, gold, platinum group elements and potentially diamonds. Natural Resources Minister Anthony Lynham said the discovery could expand understanding of Queensland’s mineral potential and support technologies such as fuel cells, mobile phones, super-conducting magnets and hybrid vehicle batteries.

The New Jersey Superior Court considered whether an employee’s sick pay and wages for personal and family illness days are collateral sources deductible from a lost-wages claim under N.J.S.A. 2A:15-97. Plaintiff sought lost wages after an auto accident, while defendant argued that paid leave benefits should be disclosed and offset. Relying on the statute’s purpose of preventing duplicate recovery and persuasive authority from other jurisdictions, the court held that using earned leave requires the employee to surrender benefits available for future illness, injury, childcare, or retirement cash-out. Therefore, such payments are not duplicate benefits and cannot be set off against plaintiff’s lost-wages recovery.

The passage argues that Ontario’s K–12 education system excludes disabled, racialized, and marginalized students despite claims of inclusion. It frames current special education practices as insufficient because students are often placed in systems that do not ensure belonging, meaningful participation, or responsiveness to their needs. It also states that educators face barriers such as limited resources, inadequate training on disability, large class sizes, reduced funding, and policy constraints.

The paper defines terminology related to disability, including people-first language, disabled identity, and the distinction between inclusive and exclusive education. It uses UNESCO’s definition of inclusion as all children learning together regardless of differences, while exclusive education separates disabled students from non-disabled peers.

The history section traces special education in Ontario from 19th-century residential institutions and segregated classes to later special day classes and the integration movement influenced by civil rights advocacy. It also discusses multicultural and anti-racist education in Ontario, noting that racialized students remain overrepresented in some special education categories and underrepresented in gifted, learning disability, and autism diagnoses.

The passage explains that Individual Education Plans and school-based disability identification are used to determine supports and placements, but it critiques these processes for relying on deficit-based labels and excluding students from key decisions. It outlines placement types ranging from regular classes with support to full special education classes.

A major concern is lack of planning for disabled and marginalized learners. The passage critiques Ontario’s Policy on Accessible Education for Students with Disabilities, arguing that policy claims are not consistently reflected in practice and that educators lack guidance, training, and funding to implement inclusive education. This study developed and validated a two-week, six-hour Critical Multicultural Education (CME) learning module for pre-service English language teachers in Türkiye. Using a qualitative design, the module was created through four stages: researcher brainstorming, feedback from a critical friend, small-group implementation, and larger-group implementation. It was first tested online with 15 pre-service teachers from several Turkish universities, then revised and implemented with 86 students at Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University. Findings showed that the module helped participants develop more positive attitudes toward diversity, gain perspectives on social issues, and increase awareness of educational goals, ideologies behind education, the political nature of teaching, material development, lesson planning, and the implementation of CME in English language teaching. Participants also reported gaining pedagogical insights and exposure to new teaching resources and critical discussion practices.

The main challenges were limited time, dense content, teacher-centeredness, and insufficient focus on critical action. Despite these limitations, the module was found effective in broadening pre-service teachers’ understanding of diversity, social inequalities, critical approaches to education, and critical multicultural education. The study argues that CME can contribute to English language teacher education, especially in contexts where pre-service teachers have limited prior exposure to critical pedagogy or CME.

Digital leaders build strong data cultures by adopting a growth mindset, using data to create shared context, empowering teams to examine data, and aligning organizations around common targets. They encourage sensible risk-taking, experimentation, and long-term employee development, treating failures as learning opportunities while using planning and controls to manage risk. Digital laggards tend to prioritize short-term needs, optimize existing processes, discourage risk-taking, and provide narrow, transactional training.

Digital leaders emphasize transparency in data and decision-making, making relevant data widely available to support collaboration and problem solving while maintaining governance for privacy, ethics, and protection. Digital laggards often restrict data access, store data in silos, rely on judgment or individual expertise, and use data mainly to justify decisions already made. Research cited in the passage found that 88% of digital leaders have standardized APIs enabling data flow between departments, compared with 27% of digital laggards.

Digital leaders use measurement to learn, set realistic but ambitious data-driven goals, track progress, and combine metrics with reviews. Clear goals and metrics often give teams flexibility and autonomy in how they achieve outcomes. Digital laggards struggle to ground objectives in data, often set aspirational goals employees view as unrealistic, and substitute qualitative process adherence for objective measures, which can stifle innovation.

Digital leaders connect metrics and objectives to organizational strategy, creating shared goals that align teams vertically and horizontally. They often use transparent, combined top-down and bottom-up goal-setting processes to build buy-in. Digital laggards often fail to connect goals clearly to strategy, leading to misalignment and deprioritized objectives.

The passage argues that data culture is central to digital transformation. Digital leaders align beliefs, values, and daily behaviors around learning, transparency, measurement, and risk-taking, while laggards often recognize the importance of data culture but are held back by entrenched habits, skill gaps, and insufficient leadership focus. Organizations may fall into four patterns: data novice, insight ready, tech enabled, or data reliant, each requiring targeted actions to strengthen data culture.

The lecture introduces linearized general relativity as the first method for solving the Einstein field equations, alongside symmetric solutions and numerical solutions. The Einstein equations are treated as nonlinear differential equations for the spacetime metric, complicated by the metric’s appearance both in curvature terms and in matter sources such as perfect fluids.

Linearized gravity applies to weak fields, where the metric is written as flat spacetime plus a small perturbation, and all terms quadratic or higher in the perturbation are neglected. In nearly Lorentz coordinates, the perturbation can be treated mathematically like a tensor field on flat spacetime. Lorentz transformations leave the flat background unchanged while transforming the perturbation like a flat-spacetime tensor. Indices on perturbations are raised and lowered with the flat metric, and the inverse metric is the flat inverse minus the perturbation to linear order.

The lecture discusses infinitesimal coordinate transformations, which shift the metric perturbation by derivatives of the transformation generator. These gauge transformations leave the linearized Riemann tensor unchanged, analogous to electromagnetic gauge transformations leaving fields unchanged. The Riemann, Ricci, Ricci scalar, and Einstein tensor are then expressed to linear order in the metric perturbation.

A trace-reversed perturbation is introduced to simplify the Einstein tensor. By choosing the Lorentz gauge, where the divergence of the trace-reversed perturbation vanishes, the linearized Einstein equations reduce to a wave equation for the trace-reversed perturbation sourced by the stress-energy tensor. This has the same mathematical structure as the Lorentz-gauge wave equation in electrodynamics.

In the static, nonrelativistic perfect-fluid limit, the dominant stress-energy component is the mass density. The field equation reduces to the Newtonian Poisson equation, showing that the trace-reversed time-time perturbation is proportional to the Newtonian gravitational potential. This yields the Newtonian limit metric of general relativity, which underlies many weak-field tests and applications such as gravitational lensing, solar-system corrections, and many binary systems. The lecture also notes that rotating bodies produce additional gravity from mass currents, leading to gravitomagnetic effects. Future lectures will address general linearized solutions, dynamic sources, and gravitational radiation.

The TPS7H500x-SP series provides fixed-frequency, peak current mode PWM control for space-grade DC-DC converters. Internal oscillator operation supports 100 kHz to 2 MHz switching, with SYNC outputting twice the switching frequency.

The controllers support configurable primary and synchronous rectifier outputs depending on device variant. External gate drivers are recommended due to roughly 150-mA peak output capability. Dead time, leading-edge blanking, duty-cycle limits, slope compensation, current sensing, hiccup overcurrent protection, external fault shutdown, and thermal shutdown are described. Pulse skipping is used when minimum on-time limitations occur, including during high-frequency operation.

The passage also outlines compensation design using Type 2A or Type 2B networks, current-limit resistor selection, hiccup timing, and supported converter topologies including buck, flyback, forward, active-clamp forward, push-pull, and full-bridge. A synchronous push-pull design example using TPS7H5001-SP and GaN devices provides component-selection guidance for switching frequency, feedback resistors, dead time, blanking time, soft start, transformer, FETs, clamps, output filter, current sensing, hiccup capacitor, compensation, and slope compensation.

Power supply recommendations specify a 4-V to 14-V input range with proper bypassing. Layout guidance emphasizes separating analog and power grounds, minimizing high-current and switching loops, routing sensitive traces away from noisy nodes, placing bypass and compensation components close to the controller, filtering CS_ILIM as needed, and handling package-specific grounding. The passage also lists related documentation, support resources, revision history, mechanical and packaging information, and TI disclaimers.

The lecture examines Schwarzschild spacetime as a vacuum solution with mass, noting a true tidal singularity at r = 0 and a coordinate singularity at r = 2GM. Infalling bodies cross r = 2GM in finite proper time but never reach it in Schwarzschild coordinate time. Light emitted near r = 2GM becomes infinitely redshifted for distant observers, showing that the Schwarzschild time coordinate fails there.

By studying radial null geodesics, the lecture shows that Schwarzschild light cones collapse near r = 2GM. Alternative coordinates are introduced: tortoise coordinates, ingoing and outgoing null coordinates, and Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates. These remove the coordinate pathology at r = 2GM and reveal that all future-directed timelike paths inside r = 2GM lead toward r = 0. The surface r = 2GM is therefore an event horizon, beyond which events cannot causally affect the exterior; such a spacetime is a black hole.

The lecture also discusses other black hole solutions. The Reissner-Nordstrom solution describes a charged black hole and can yield a naked singularity if charge exceeds mass in the stated units. The Kerr solution describes a spinning black hole, with an event horizon determined by its spin parameter, and includes frame-dragging-like effects that distinguish prograde and retrograde orbits. The Kerr-Newman solution combines mass, spin, and charge.

The No-Hair theorem states that stationary 3+1-dimensional spacetimes with event horizons are Kerr-Newman black holes, fully characterized by mass, spin, and charge. In astrophysical contexts, charge is rapidly neutralized, so observed black holes are described by Kerr. During collapse or merger, radiation removes deviations from Kerr-Newman form, a behavior associated with Price’s theorem.

The ADS9803 provides a source-synchronous data interface with output data and capture clock on DCLKOUT; data clock frequency depends on sampling clock speed, SDR/DDR mode, number of lanes, and frame clock frequency. It includes data output randomization using XOR with either a PRBS bit or ADC LSB to reduce correlation between data transmission ground bounce and analog input voltage. It supports simple averaging, which halves output data rate, and moving averaging, which does not.

The device provides fixed, ramp, and alternating digital test patterns for channel groups CH[4:1] and CH[8:5]. It can be reset through the RESET pin or register field, powered down through the PWDN pin or PD_CH field, and must be initialized after reset or power-up with a register-write sequence while a free-running sampling clock is present. Speed-boost mode allows up to 8MSPS on a selected analog input channel pair while other channels remain idle.

Configuration uses 16-bit registers in three banks accessed through SPI, with bank selection through register 0x03. SPI read access requires enabling SPI_RD_EN and SPI_MODE, and daisy-chain SPI supports multiple ADCs with shared CS and SCLK and delayed data passing through devices. California lawmakers revived a proposal to require 100 percent carbon-free energy by 2045 and sent it to the full Assembly for a vote later this year. The bill, authored by Democratic Sen. The paper presents a Rocq formalization of constructive nominal sets as a foundation for a nominal framework, closely following an Agda development while using Rocq typeclasses and generalized rewriting to reduce the burden of setoids. Nominal sets model name dependence through finite permutations, support, freshness, α-equivalence, name abstraction, and finitely supported functions. In the constructive setting, least supports are replaced by arbitrary supports, and freshness is defined through swaps with fresh names; existential and universal formulations are related by some/any principles.

The Rocq development defines atoms as an abstract type with decidable equality and infinitude, implemented by natural numbers. Permutations are represented as lists of swaps, with composition by concatenation and inverse by list reversal, treated as a setoid because representations are not unique. Nominal sets are specified through a typeclass hierarchy with permutation actions, support functions, equivalence relations, and support laws.

The development formalizes constructive freshness, name abstraction using a dedicated record type, finitely supported functions as bundled records, the Freshness Theorem, and the Freshness Condition for Binders. The Freshness Theorem was not present in the earlier Agda work. The formalization avoids assuming functional extensionality by using setoids and relies on typeclass-based rewriting to manage equivalence reasoning.

The authors relate their work to Isabelle’s nominal package, prior Rocq and Agda developments, and recent Agda work on permutation representations. Future work aims at deriving α-structural recursion and induction principles, with an α-recursion principle for the λ-calculus already derived and alternatives for induction under investigation.

Netflix grew from a 1997 mail-order DVD rental company into the leading global streaming-video provider, reaching 167 million paid subscribers and a $157 billion enterprise value by 2019. Its growth came through licensed content, international expansion, heavy investment in original programming, and a corporate culture emphasizing high-performing employees, decentralized decision-making, candor, transparency, and few rules.

By 2019, competition intensified as major media companies ended licensing deals, consolidated assets, and launched rival streaming services, including Disney+. Netflix relied increasingly on original content, spending $15 billion in 2019, while maintaining a strategy focused on ad-free, subscription-based streaming.

India became central to Netflix’s growth ambitions, with executives describing it as the source of the company’s “next 100 million” subscribers. Netflix entered India in 2016, but by 2019 had only about two million users there, compared with Disney+ Hotstar’s rapid growth. India’s streaming market was price-sensitive, mobile-driven, highly competitive, and dominated by services offering low-cost or ad-supported plans, local-language content, and large regional libraries.

Netflix responded by launching a $2.85 mobile-only plan and increasing investment in Indian content, planning $420 million in local production and licensing by the end of 2020. The case raises strategic questions about whether Netflix should adapt its premium pricing, ad-free model, content focus, acquisition stance, and decentralized decision-making to succeed in India.

The DISCARD operation lets SDHC and SDXC cards partially or fully de-allocate specified write blocks, with discarded contents treated as “don’t care.” Hosts use CMD32, CMD33, then CMD38 with argument 00000001h, only if DISCARD_SUPPORT is set. Out-of-sequence or out-of-range commands set errors and reset the sequence. DISCARD is not supported over SPI, and busy timeout is 250 ms.

The passage describes stackless native assembler procedures that use register passing to initialize and later remove a pre-memory stack region. The stack initialization routine sets up processor/cache state, divides the pre-memory stack among cores, maps it to global address space, sets MTRRs on x86-64, creates a UEFI_SEC_PEI_HAND_OFF instance, and must run on all cores. It handles protected mode and real mode differently for SS:ESP setup and returns success, warning for stack reentry, or fatal error for unknown processor family.

The stack removal routine disables Cache-as-RAM after main memory and stack relocation are available, flushes cache lines, preserves EBX, and must be run on all cores but invoked only by the BSP. It returns success when stack space is disabled. AARCH64 APUs with PSP do not use these stack and early macros because the PSP initializes DRAM.

The passage also describes AmdCreateStruct, which allocates and initializes AGESA parameter structures using pre-memory heap, post-memory DRAM, or host-provided storage. It requires an established stack and returns success, allocation/size error, or fatal initialization failure.

Another procedure returns normalized DIMM data eye bitmaps for specified socket, channel, and read/write direction, requiring operational coherent HyperTransport links and a stack.

RADAR is a framework for routing queries to reasoning language model configurations that balance performance and cost. It treats each model and reasoning-budget pair as a configuration, predicts whether a configuration can answer a query correctly, and selects one using multi-objective optimization over performance and cost. RADAR uses Item Response Theory to estimate query difficulty and configuration ability from evaluation data, with query embeddings supporting generalization to unseen and out-of-distribution queries. It operates in a black-box, plug-and-play setting, requires no model fine-tuning, adds low latency, and can incorporate new configurations through adaptive calibration. Experiments on challenging reasoning benchmarks show that RADAR achieves stronger performance-cost tradeoffs than existing routing methods, including matching much of the performance of stronger configurations at substantially lower cost.

President Obama delivers a farewell address in Chicago, thanking Americans for making him a better President and person. He reflects on beginning his public life in Chicago and says change happens when ordinary people get involved. He describes American democracy as a continuing effort to expand equality, rights, and the common good.

He cites achievements from his presidency, including recovery from recession, job creation, the auto industry’s rebound, a new relationship with Cuba, the Iran nuclear agreement, the killing of Osama bin Laden, marriage equality, and expanded health insurance. Obama argues that democracy faces major challenges: economic inequality, racial division, retreat into partisan and media “bubbles,” denial of shared facts, terrorism, authoritarianism, and taking democratic institutions for granted. The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court’s ruling that Vigilant Insurance Company was primarily responsible for Essex Source Realty Group’s $87,500 share of a settled injury claim brought by Jill Kearns. A University of Bonn study found that male African cichlids exposed to predator alarm substances grow faster and delay developing conspicuous breeding coloration. Researchers raised two groups under identical conditions, adding conspecific extract containing alarm substances to one group. Males in the predator-risk group developed larger bodies, larger eyes, longer dorsal fin spines, and paler coloration at the onset of sexual maturity, likely reducing predation risk. The effects were observed only in males, possibly because males remain outside breeding caves to defend territory while females care for eggs inside. By about one year of age, males in both groups showed similarly conspicuous coloration, which functions in dominance signaling and mate attraction.

Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) is recurring depression linked to seasonal changes, most often appearing in fall or winter and improving in spring or summer; summer SAD is rare. It affects an estimated 1–10% of the global population, is more common farther from the equator, affects more women than men, and often begins in young adulthood. Scientists believe reduced sunlight may disrupt serotonin, melatonin, mood, and sleep patterns, though some question whether SAD exists. Symptoms of winter SAD include fatigue, difficulty waking, cravings, weight gain, poor concentration, depression, social withdrawal, low sex drive, and aches; summer SAD may involve insomnia, appetite loss, weight loss, and anxiety. Untreated SAD can worsen and contribute to serious mental health problems. Treatments include light therapy, medication, psychotherapy, meditation, and relaxation techniques. Because other conditions can resemble SAD, physician consultation is recommended. Preventive measures include exercise, outdoor time, social activity, regular sleep, balanced diet, stress reduction, full-spectrum lighting, plants, and added color.

The Arms Index, or TRIN, is a market sentiment indicator created by Richard W. Arms in 1967 to assess market strength or weakness by comparing advancing and declining stocks with advancing and declining volume. A reading of 1.0 indicates balance, below 1.0 is generally viewed as bullish, and above 1.0 as bearish. Extreme readings above 3.0 may indicate oversold conditions and possible bullish reversal, while readings below 0.50 may indicate overbought conditions.

The passage explains related concepts including AD Volume, advancing and declining volume, and market breadth, noting that volume-based breadth indicators can reveal buying or selling pressure within an index. It states that TRIN can be useful but should not be used alone and should be backtested with other indicators.

Backtests described in the passage found that a simple TRIN strategy produced 522 trades with an average gain of 0.39% per trade and was not considered tradable as-is. Adding a second indicator improved the average gain to 0.66%, with a 77% win rate and a 2.4 profit factor, suggesting TRIN added value when combined with another indicator.

U.S. meat consumption may reach record levels in 2018, but the composition has changed significantly over time. Per capita beef consumption peaked in the 1970s and has fallen by about one-third, while chicken consumption has more than doubled and surpassed beef around 1990. This shift reduces environmental pressure because beef requires far more land and emits more greenhouse gases than chicken, though plant-based foods have even lower impacts.

Factors behind the shift from beef to chicken include health concerns, more women in the workforce, greater availability of ready-to-cook chicken, increased chicken production efficiency, and lower chicken prices. Recent rebounds in meat and beef consumption may be linked to lower feed prices, increased production, and recovery from the Great Recession.

Beef remains the largest contributor to Americans’ dietary environmental footprint and U.S. beef consumption is still far above the world average. The passage argues that further shifts toward plant-based foods are needed to meet climate and sustainability goals, and notes that WRI will release modeling on dietary shifts needed by 2050.

The passage proposes Pilot-and-Adaptive Stable Trading (PAST), a framework for resource trading in edge-assisted UAV networks with spatio-temporal dynamism. It addresses limitations of online trading, including high negotiation overhead, transaction failures, UAV mobility, fluctuating task demands, and variable edge server resources. PAST combines PilotAO, which establishes futures-style pilot trading agreements with risk-aware overbooking through stable many-to-many matching, and AdaptAO, which uses double deep Q-learning to update agreements and overbooking rates during operation.

The model defines UAVs as service buyers with computing tasks and edge servers as sellers with limited resources also serving inherent requestors. PilotAO considers expected utilities, payments, penalties, service costs, task feasibility, and risks for both UAVs and edge servers. It aims to ensure individual rationality, strong stability, competitive equilibrium, and weak Pareto optimality. AdaptAO monitors agreement fulfillment, resource demand, UAV locations, utilities, interactions, and reputation to decide whether to renew agreements and adjust overbooking rates.

Experiments using the Chicago taxi trip dataset compare PAST with spot trading, non-adaptive futures trading, futures trading without overbooking, greedy matching, and random matching. Results show that PAST reduces decision overhead and task completion latency compared with spot trading, improves social welfare over static futures approaches, increases resource utilization through overbooking and adaptation, maintains higher task completion under pilot agreements, and satisfies individual rationality for UAVs and edge servers. Future work includes privacy preservation, machine-learning-based task specification, and extension to heterogeneous multi-UAV and multi-edge-server networks.

The lecture discusses empirical research on price discrimination, focusing on whether firms discriminate, whether pricing patterns match profit-maximizing models, the size of profit gains, effects on consumer surplus, and the role of online information.

Early studies examined whether price differences reflected costs or discrimination. Borenstein argued that the price gap between leaded and unleaded gasoline was too large to be cost-based. Shepard found evidence of second-degree price discrimination between self-service and full-service gasoline. Studies of racial and gender price discrimination produced mixed results: Ayres and Siegelman found large discrimination in car bargaining against women and minorities, Goldberg found no racial price differences using Consumer Expenditure Survey data, and Graddy found Asians paid less than whites at the Fulton Street Fish Market.

Scott Morton, Zettelmeyer, and Silva-Risso used Autobytel and JD Power car transaction data to reexamine car pricing. They found statistically significant but much smaller demographic price differences than earlier audit studies: buyers in Black and Hispanic areas paid more, Asian buyers paid less, and women paid slightly more. More educated and homeowner areas paid less, suggesting differences may relate to search ability or bargaining sophistication. Autobytel buyers paid less overall, and demographic gaps were largely reduced among online buyers.

The lecture then examines online price discrimination. Shiller used ComScore web browsing data to estimate Netflix demand without price variation, relying on observed costs and profit maximization assumptions. He found demographic targeting would raise Netflix profits only about 0.3%, while web browsing-based targeting could raise profits about 13%. Demographic targeting slightly increased consumer surplus, while web browsing targeting slightly reduced it. He also argued second-degree discrimination through plan design could be more important than third-degree discrimination.

Dubé and Misra studied ZipRecruiter using randomized pricing experiments. ZipRecruiter charged small employers $99 per month, but experimental variation showed short-run profits would be higher at much higher uniform prices, with an estimated optimal price of $327. Personalized pricing based on 133 firm and job features could increase profits by about 8.2% relative to the optimal uniform price but would reduce consumer surplus substantially and lower social welfare in their model. A follow-up experiment confirmed their pricing predictions, though ZipRecruiter adopted a higher uniform price rather than personalized prices.

The lecture concludes that empirical evidence shows price discrimination exists, but demographic discrimination often appears small. Online behavioral data can be more useful for targeting, though estimated profit gains may still be limited and firms may avoid personalization due to practical, reputational, or broader market concerns.

Research software is central to modern science, but many research-performing organisations lack coherent policies to support its development, sustainability, legal and ethical use, and recognition. Existing institutional attention often appears in open science, infrastructure, or licensing policies, but research software is frequently mentioned only briefly and is rarely integrated into research assessment, hiring, promotion, or reward structures.

The Policies in Research Organisations for Research Software (PRO4RS) Working Group, a 2023–2025 joint initiative of ReSA and RDA, examined how institutions can develop, align, and implement research software policies. Its outputs include a global list of public institutional policies, reports on enabling policy change and identifying policy gaps, and case studies of four organisations. The group defines research software as source code, algorithms, scripts, workflows, and executables created during or for research.

The analysis found major gaps in policy support for research software personnel and assessment reform. Broader initiatives such as DORA, CoARA, Science Europe, OpenAIRE, OPUS, SHARC, and the Amsterdam Declaration support recognition of diverse research outputs and roles, including software and software engineers, but implementation remains difficult due to limited suitable metrics and longstanding academic evaluation practices.

PRO4RS recommends a layered approach: optionally create a dedicated research software policy; align related policies on open science, intellectual property, legal and ethical use, communities, training, hiring, evaluation, and promotion; and connect policies to practical guidelines and frameworks. It also recommends that institutions document the volume of research software they produce, advocate for its role in research, and engage institutional stakeholders to include research software in broader research quality and excellence policies.

Following President Tyler’s 1842 recommendation, Congress funded a diplomatic officer to the Sandwich Islands, and George Brown was appointed commissioner in 1843. He sought equal, nonexclusive treatment for U.S. citizens, which the King affirmed. Relations soon deteriorated over the John Wiley case, in which an American was denied jury trial, while French and British treaties granted such rights to their nationals. Brown protested perceived discrimination, and the King requested his recall, though the U.S. approved his conduct and appointed Mr. Ten Eyck.

In 1844, Mr. Calhoun confirmed U.S. recognition of Hawaiian independence. France and Britain concluded new conventions in 1846 modifying earlier jury and liquor provisions, though these did not appear to fully recognize Hawaiian independence. Denmark’s 1846 treaty included a favored-nation clause and was described as the first unrestricted acknowledgment of Hawaiian independence.

Ten Eyck was instructed to negotiate a treaty but persisted in seeking an objectionable jury clause despite guidance from Mr. Buchanan. Negotiations failed, while other nations gained treaty advantages. Ten Eyck became embroiled in disputes over American residents’ rights and was criticized by Buchanan. He resigned in 1848, and Charles Fames was appointed in 1849.

The passage examines a qualitative case study on using community oral history projects to support elementary preservice teachers’ learning and future teaching of citizenship education. It argues that citizenship is central to social studies but is often marginalized in elementary classrooms, while preservice teachers may enter preparation programs with limited or confused understandings of citizenship. The study positions oral history as an inquiry-based strategy that can connect citizenship to dialogue, controversial topics, historical thinking, diversity, emotions, community engagement, and interdisciplinary learning.

The study involved 38 elementary preservice teachers in four undergraduate K–6 social studies methods courses at a South Florida university. Participants selected citizenship-related topics, interviewed community members with relevant lived experiences, researched their topics, created open-ended questions, used technology to record or transcribe interviews, and completed post-project reflections. Interview topics included immigration, military service, entrepreneurship, poverty, civil rights, 9/11, natural disasters, workplace discrimination, gender equality, and global conflict.

Findings indicated that the project helped preservice teachers gain deeper content knowledge, recognize multiple perspectives, connect historical and contemporary issues, and understand topics beyond textbook or media accounts. Many reported personal emotional impact, increased empathy, appreciation for community members and elders, and motivation toward civic action. Participants also stated that the experience would influence their future teaching by encouraging them to use oral histories, invite community speakers, address difficult topics, and help students engage more deeply with citizenship.

The passage concludes that community oral histories provided preservice teachers with a more humanistic and authentic understanding of citizenship and democracy. It suggests that oral history can become meaningful coursework in social studies methods courses and recommends future research on professional development, pre-surveys, and how these preservice teachers later use oral history with elementary students.

The passage introduces FishNet++, a large-scale multimodal benchmark for marine species recognition, created to evaluate whether state-of-the-art vision-language and multimodal large language models can support marine ecology conservation. Aquatic biodiversity monitoring is difficult due to inaccessible environments and the need for expert identification. The authors find that current models perform poorly on fine-grained fish species recognition: Qwen2.5-VL reaches 6.2% accuracy on frequent species and 0.2% on rare species, while GPT-4o performs better but remains limited.

FishNet++ contains 99,556 images across 17,393 fish species, 35,133 textual species descriptions, 119,399 bounding boxes, and 706,426 key-point annotations. It expands and corrects the original FishNet dataset with updated taxonomy, added images, expert-guided key-part annotations, and descriptions generated from sources including FishBase, iNaturalist, WoRMS, and NOAA. The dataset supports open-vocabulary recognition, detection, and key-part localization.

Diagnostic experiments show that model failures arise from multiple sources. Qwen2.5-VL performs poorly on translating between common and scientific names, indicating limited marine taxonomic knowledge. It can distinguish random incorrect species better than chance but struggles with visually similar alternatives, showing weak visual domain knowledge. It performs reasonably on coarse fish localization but poorly on fine-grained key-part localization, which is important for species-level distinctions.

Fine-tuning improves performance. LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL on FishNet++ raises species accuracy on frequent species from 6.2% to 37.0%, with stronger genus and family-level results. Ensemble retrieval-augmented generation provides smaller gains. Explainable fine-tuning produces species predictions with supporting reasoning while maintaining similar accuracy, improving interpretability for marine science use.

The passage describes power, reset, clocking, interrupt, and peripheral features of the TMS320DM814x DaVinci Digital Media Processors.

SRAM blocks can enter SHUTDOWN mode to reduce leakage, removing voltage and losing data; SRAM in switchable power domains shuts down when the domain is OFF. Some ALWAYS_ON SRAM can be independently powered down through Control Module registers. The device supports multiple I/O voltage groups at 1.8 V or 3.3 V, DDR I/O at 1.5 V or 1.8 V, PHY power-down modes, and Low-Power Standby Mode with switchable domains OFF, ARM Cortex-A8 in an IDLE loop, and unused blocks clock gated. Power supplies are organized into sequencing groups, and specified power-up/power-down sequences must be followed. PLL and analog supplies require filtering, and decoupling capacitors should be placed close to power pins.

The device supports several resets, including power-on reset, external warm reset, emulation warm reset, watchdog reset, software global cold and warm resets, test reset, local resets, and reset isolation for PCIe and the EMAC Switch. Reset behavior affects pin states, boot mode latching, ARM Cortex-A8 boot from ROM, PRCM reset control, and the RSTOUT_WD_OUT pin. Power domains have dedicated warm and cold resets, and most I/O pins enter Hi-Z during reset except specified exceptions.

Clocking uses DEV and AUX inputs, internal oscillators or 1.8-V LVCMOS inputs, SERDES differential reference clocks, optional audio and 32768-Hz clocks, selectable CLKOUT outputs, 12 top-level PLLs, and 4 embedded PLLs. PLLs start in bypass mode after reset and must meet defined frequency limits. SYSCLK and module clock frequencies must remain within specified limits.

The ARM Cortex-A8 interrupt controller handles up to 128 programmable interrupt requests, while the C674x DSP interrupt controller combines up to 128 events into 12 prioritized CPU interrupts with optional multiplexing. Peripheral sections cover DCAN, EDMA, advanced event triggering, trace, JTAG, EMAC Switch, MDIO, GPIO, GPMC/ELM, HDMI, and HDVPSS. These include functional descriptions, register mappings, timing requirements, routing and ESD guidance, and interface capabilities such as Ethernet modes, GPIO interrupt generation, external memory support, HDMI 1.3a transmission, and HD video input/output processing.

NVIDIA GA10x Ampere GPUs provide second-generation RT Cores and third-generation Tensor Cores, offering up to 2x improvements in programmable shading, ray tracing, and AI over prior architectures. GeForce RTX 30-series GPUs use GA10x architecture for ray-traced gaming, AI features such as DLSS, GDDR6X memory, and RTX IO for faster SSD-to-GPU asset loading and decompression. It supports real-time and final-frame ray tracing, hardware-accelerated motion blur, AI denoising, large 3D datasets, and professional certifications. The passage also describes GDDR6X Error Detection and Replay, which detects memory transmission errors and retries transactions during overclocking.

The lecture reviews relativistic kinematics for nuclear and particle physics, where particles often move near the speed of light. It defines beta as velocity in units of c, gamma as \(1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\), total energy as \(\gamma mc^2\), momentum as \(\gamma mv\), and the relation \(E^2=p^2+m^2\). For massless particles, energy equals momentum; for particles at rest, energy equals mass.

Lorentz transformations are discussed, including the distinction between invariant quantities, which do not change under transformations, and conserved quantities, such as total energy and momentum in reactions. The invariant mass of a system can be calculated from the total energy and momentum of decay products and used to identify a parent particle, as in Higgs boson decays to photon pairs.

The lecture compares fixed-target and collider experiments, using Z boson production as an example. In electron-positron colliders such as LEP, two beams of about 45.5 GeV each can produce a 91 GeV Z boson, while a fixed-target setup would require analysis to determine the needed positron beam energy.

Several exercises illustrate applications of relativistic kinematics: computing gamma factors at LEP, finding deuteron binding energy from particle masses, analyzing photon emission and absorption, determining the energy needed to produce antiprotons or pions in proton collisions, calculating decay product speeds from pion decay at rest, and studying Compton scattering. The focus is on using kinematics to determine energies and momenta without yet considering underlying dynamics, forces, lifetimes, or decay probabilities.

Sean Combs was sentenced to 50 months in prison, closing his criminal case but leaving him with dozens of civil lawsuits and severe reputational damage. He denies sexual assault accusations. Public trial evidence may support future civil claims, with more lawsuits expected. His business empire has declined, including lost partnerships, brands, and media stakes, while experts say his former status is unlikely to recover.

The President returns Senate bill No. 71, concerning Chinese immigration, with objections. He argues that nations should repudiate treaty obligations only for paramount interests and after seeking mutual modification. He says the 1880 treaty with China allowed the United States to regulate, limit, or suspend Chinese labor immigration, but not absolutely prohibit it, and that any limitation must be reasonable. He concludes that the bill’s twenty-year suspension of Chinese laborers amounts to an unreasonable prohibition and breaches national faith.

He also questions provisions requiring Chinese registration and passports, calling them undemocratic and possibly inconsistent with treaty protections for exempt classes such as teachers, students, merchants, and travelers. He notes the bill lacks provision for Chinese subjects transiting across the United States. While agreeing that some legislation is necessary, he urges a shorter experimental suspension, citing treaty obligations, possible labor needs in some regions, and the importance of maintaining friendly commercial relations with China and Asia.

A tuna-fishing group about 120 kilometres off Tofino, including former Vancouver Canuck Willie Mitchell, encountered a large shark they first thought was a great white. GoPro footage helped identify it as an eight- to nine-foot salmon shark, a species related to great whites but generally timid and focused on Pacific salmon. Vancouver Aquarium biologist Ruby Banwait said sightings are rare and indicate a healthy ecosystem, as sharks help remove sick or injured animals. Mitchell said the encounter was unsettling because he had swum in the same waters earlier. Experts note warming waters could bring more southern shark species, including great whites, farther north.

German MP Norbert Röttgen urged the EU to formally suspend Turkey membership talks, citing Erdogan’s growing authoritarian rule. Erdogan dismissed European threats to freeze talks as unimportant after tensions with European leaders during Turkey’s campaign.

NVIDIA Corporation filed a Form 8-K with the SEC on August 8, 2022, reporting that it issued a press release announcing selected preliminary financial results for the second quarter ended July 31, 2022. Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.

Academics in Zimbabwe and South Africa criticized Grace Mugabe’s 2014 University of Zimbabwe PhD, saying it fails doctoral standards. The thesis, posted online four years late, was accused of plagiarism, relying on grey literature and outdated sources, lacking original contribution, and citing works from after her graduation. Some UZ academics petitioned the anti-corruption commission, though no investigation was underway. Rhodes University sociologist Kirk Helliker said its theory discussion was extremely shallow and far below PhD expectations.

Wall Street indexes closed higher Monday, led by technology and energy, as oil prices rose and investors awaited an expected Federal Reserve rate hike. Apple boosted technology stocks, while energy gained after a North Sea pipeline shutdown lifted oil prices. The Dow rose 0.23%, the S&P 500 gained 0.32%, and the Nasdaq added 0.51%. Traders saw an 85% chance of a 25 basis point Fed hike. Healthcare stocks drew attention after blood disorder drug data, with Bluebird Bio jumping 17.9%. Bitcoin-related stocks also surged after the debut of bitcoin futures trading. Markets appeared to shrug off an attempted attack at a New York commuter hub.

MIT CSAIL researchers led by Mohammad Alizadeh developed Pensieve, an AI system that uses a neural network to improve video streaming by choosing algorithms based on network conditions. In tests, it reduced rebuffering by 10–30% and improved quality by 10–25%. Pensieve can prioritize quality, speed, or data conservation. The team is open-sourcing the code and plans to test it on VR video.

In Causey v. Wolfe, the Arkansas court affirmed the chancery court’s decree. It held that Eugene A. Causey acquired fee simple title to the section 16 lands through a prior chancery decree based on Isaac Adair’s gift, Causey’s possession, and improvements, and that the decree bound Causey’s children even though they were not yet born. A promise to give land and complete title was treated as a promise to convey the whole estate, not merely a life estate. The court also held that Causey held only a life estate in the section 15 lands under Adair’s will, with remainder to his children. Because timber was removed from that tract, the Tillar estate was liable for waste, but only for one-fourth of the timber’s actual value, or $154.84, since 25 percent should have been left for farm upkeep.

Two years after being traded from the Maple Leafs to the Penguins, Phil Kessel celebrated his second Stanley Cup win by golfing and eating hot dogs from the Cup, referencing past criticism with an Instagram caption: “Hotdogs taste better out of The Cup! #twotime.”

The study reports nanoscale water-permeable structural defects at merging regions between aligned graphene flakes grown by ambient-pressure CVD on single-crystal Cu(111)/sapphire. Although such single-orientation stitching is often expected to be seamless and impermeable, SEM and AFM revealed two merging behaviors: regions without visible lines and regions with clear phase-contrast merging lines. Raman mapping after hot-water oxidation showed Cu2O formation beneath some merging regions, indicating water-permeable pathways; about 45% of 122 merging regions were defective, while about 55% appeared seamless. Conductive AFM confirmed that some flakes on both sides of merging lines had aligned lattice orientations. STM showed that some merging lines are overlapped junctions where one graphene edge lies atop another rather than forming a continuous in-plane stitch. The authors classify merging as seamless stitching, defective stitching, or overlapped junctions, and suggest these defects may be relevant for filtration, desalination, and molecular sieving applications.

The passage discusses public and media reactions to alleged or confirmed sex scandals involving women in politics, focusing on Nikki Haley rumors and Nashville Mayor Megan Barry’s admitted affair with a subordinate, Sgt. Robert Forrest Jr. It contrasts responses to Barry’s consensual affair with #MeToo-related scandals, noting defenses that men in power often face less scrutiny for affairs. The author argues Barry’s public handling emphasized embarrassment, faith, consent, limited details, and refusal to resign, framing it as a potential model for future female political sex scandals. The passage also critiques media coverage, feminist framing, and selective public outrage around such scandals.

The PGA Tour said player and fan safety is its top priority ahead of the Dell Technologies Match Play in Austin, where police are searching for a serial bomber. Security advisers are working with law enforcement. The tournament begins Wednesday at Austin Country Club, with several top golfers expected to compete.

The NCLT directed Bhushan Steel’s CoC to consider employee objections to Tata Steel’s bid at its March 20 meeting and report its decision during final approval. Employees alleged Tata Steel was an “undischarged insolvent” and ineligible under IBC Section 29A. Tata Steel opposed the application, but NCLT declined to accept its objection at this stage.

The passage describes the Office of the Historian’s ebook edition of the Foreign Relations of the United States series, noting its portability, full-text search, offline access, fidelity to print editions, and recommendation to cite document numbers. It also includes a presidential message stating that the United States is prosperous, increasingly important internationally, and facing major domestic and foreign problems. The message attributes national well-being to long-term economic forces, laws, policies, and citizenship, while urging practical regulation to address evils arising from industrial growth without halting development.

The passage introduces AutoPrune, a training-free complexity-adaptive token pruning framework for Vision-Language and Vision-Language-Action models. It addresses inefficiencies caused by long visual token sequences in high-resolution image and video inputs, where existing fixed pruning schedules fail to adapt to sample- and task-specific variation in token importance. Inspired by neuroscience, AutoPrune estimates input complexity using mutual information between early-layer visual and textual tokens, then maps it to a budget-constrained logistic retention curve. Simple inputs receive aggressive early pruning, while complex inputs retain tokens longer. The method integrates with models such as LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Senna, and reportedly outperforms prior training-free pruning methods across benchmarks, including pruning 89% of visual tokens in LLaVA-1.5-7B while retaining 96.7% average accuracy.

Singer Meghan Linsey said she was bitten on the face by a poisonous brown recluse spider while sleeping in her Nashville home on February 12. She sought urgent care after feeling stinging pain and brought the dead spider with her. Her symptoms included severe nerve pain, muscle spasms, rash, swelling, and a necrotic wound under her eye. Doctors note brown recluse bites are rare, usually not fatal, and have no antidote, with treatment focused on symptoms and wound care. Linsey received hyperbaric oxygen therapy, saw new skin develop, and said her scar is now nearly unnoticeable with makeup. She shared her experience to raise awareness.

A Nature Climate Change study finds human-driven climate change may become a leading driver of extreme summer heat waves in parts of the western U.S. as soon as the 2020s. The effect could emerge in the Great Lakes in the 2030s and the Great Plains decades later. Researchers warn population growth in the West may worsen impacts and urge mitigation and adaptation planning.

The 1-4 “Slice” zone offense uses a high alignment to create matchup problems, enable entry passes or pressure releases to four receivers, and combine inside post attacks with outside shooters. It emphasizes ball movement, quick reversals, rotations, slice cuts, post-ups, skip passes, wing entries, and counters to overplays. On post entries, the opposite post cuts to the basket, then posts up if not fed, creating high-low and baseline feed options. Weakside skip passes, extra passes, screens, and give-and-go rotations create shooting and post opportunities. Wing entries trigger slice cuts and post-up options, while reversals maintain continuity when no shot or feed is available. Against post or wing overplays, pump fakes initiate lob releases or back cuts, followed by post-ups, weakside spotting, and continued slice action.

The lecture explains policy as a “game changer” for sustainable real estate when market failures prevent alignment among environmental, social, and profit goals. It reviews two prior market failures: information asymmetry, addressed through certifications such as LEED and WELL, and split incentives between landlords and tenants, addressed through green leases. The lecture then focuses on externalities.

Positive externalities occur when green buildings create social benefits, such as reduced carbon emissions, that developers cannot fully monetize. This can lead to undersupply of green buildings. Policies can internalize these benefits through “carrots,” or incentives, such as subsidies, tax rebates, heat pump incentives, energy-efficiency programs, and density bonuses. Examples include the EU’s large renovation funding program, Massachusetts Mass Save programs, and Arlington, Virginia’s FAR bonuses for LEED-certified buildings. The lecture emphasizes that designing the right incentive level is difficult because policymakers must consider developer responses, social benefits, and social costs.

Negative externalities occur when brown buildings or polluting activities impose social costs not reflected in private costs. Policies can use “sticks,” or enforcement mechanisms, to increase private costs and reduce harmful activity. Examples include carbon taxes, penalties, disclosure requirements, building energy codes, and restrictions on leasing inefficient buildings. New York City’s building energy grades, Cambridge’s BEUDO, Boston’s BERDO, Local Law 97, and the UK’s minimum energy-efficiency leasing rules are discussed as examples.

The lecture highlights tradeoffs between sustainability and affordability. A research project with homebuilders examines Massachusetts energy-code changes and their potential effects on housing costs. Stricter requirements may reduce utility bills but increase construction costs that developers may pass on to buyers or tenants, potentially worsening affordability for certain income groups. The lecture argues that sticks may need to be paired with carrots, such as subsidies, zoning bonuses, tax rebates, or expedited permitting.

The lecture also discusses institutional responses, including MIT’s exposure to Cambridge BEUDO requirements and its net-zero goals. MIT may need to buy carbon offsets in the short term, though the offset market is described as messy and variable in quality.

The final section addresses climate-resiliency investment in coastal areas. Despite climate risks from flooding, hurricanes, heat, drought, and wildfire, people and developers continue moving into high-risk areas for reasons including jobs, taxes, cost of living, and amenities. Governments can invest in resilience strategies such as elevation, permeable surfaces, green space, and coastal protection, but these require substantial funding. Miami is presented as a wealthy city able to invest in resilience and maintain a positive feedback loop of growth and tax revenue, while Fair Bluff, North Carolina, is presented as a poorer town caught in a negative feedback loop after repeated hurricanes. Federal climate-resilience funding may create moral hazard and unequal access because poorer towns may lack the capacity or matching funds to secure support. The lecture ends by raising managed retreat as a controversial alternative to continued rebuilding in risky areas.

Workers punctured the decomposing bodies to prevent gas buildup and explosions, then trucked them to an inaccessible location. About three-quarters of the first pod of 416 died, while survivors and a second pod of about 250 were refloated. Officials remained alert for restrandings at the site, which has seen repeated whale strandings.

The passage argues that philosophy of education relies on tacit assumptions about free will, especially libertarian ideas of alternative possibilities and self-initiation, when defining autonomy, authenticity, moral responsibility, and the aims of education. It presents the dilemma of determinism: if causal determinism is true, alternative action is impossible; if indeterminism is true, actions may appear accidental and not under adequate control. In both cases, the traditional basis for autonomy and responsibility is challenged.

The text proposes Harry Frankfurt’s hierarchical theory of the will as a way to address this problem. Frankfurt’s account shifts attention from alternative possibilities to the actual structure of the will, especially second-order desires and identification with one’s will. On this view, moral responsibility can be grounded in volitional control rather than the ability to act otherwise. The passage concludes that this framework can reinterpret autonomy and authenticity in philosophy of education, avoid the paradox of moral education, and guide moral education by focusing on young people’s understanding of their will, responsibility, values, and identification with their actions.

This agreement governs software use, remains valid if any part is unenforceable, and is governed by California and U.S. federal law. Disputes must be handled in Santa Clara County courts.
