The smash concept is a widely used football passing concept suitable for all levels because it is teachable, repeatable, and effective against multiple coverages. It attacks the perimeter and provides both quick throws and downfield opportunities. It works well against man coverage, Cover 2, and Cover 4 by creating space for corner routes or allowing the quarterback to high-low defenders. Cover 3 can be problematic because flat defenders may undercut late hitch throws.

In the base concept, tight ends and slot receivers run corner routes at about 10 yards, outside receivers run 6-yard hitches, and the running back checks protection before releasing underneath. The quarterback chooses one side pre-snap based on leverage and cushion, then reads the cornerback post-snap: throw the hitch if the corner drops, throw the corner route if the corner stays low, or check down if unclear.

Variations include a 3x1 version with seam, dig, and checkdown answers against different safety looks, and a sprint-out version that moves the pocket, simplifies reads, adds a backside over route, and allows the quarterback to run if needed.

The ISM Manufacturing Index, also called the PMI, is a monthly indicator of the health of the US manufacturing sector, introduced by ISM in 1948 and published on the first business day of each month. It is based on surveys of purchasing managers at over 300 manufacturing firms and measures factors such as new orders, production, employment, supplier deliveries, and inventories. Readings above 50 indicate expansion, 50 indicates no change, and below 50 indicates contraction.

The index is closely watched by analysts, investors, traders, economists, policymakers, and businesses because it provides insight into manufacturing activity, economic growth, business conditions, and potential market impacts. It can influence stocks, indexes, currencies, bonds, and investor confidence. Businesses may use it to assess supply chains, product demand, production needs, and hiring decisions.

The PMI can be used with other economic indicators such as GDP, employment data, inflation, consumer confidence, jobless claims, and consumer spending to form a broader view of economic conditions. It is considered reliable and can provide early indications because purchasing managers may notice changes quickly, but the passage also describes it as backward-looking because it reflects prior-month activity and may already be priced into markets when released.

The PMI can be used in trading and investment strategies, including bullish strategies when readings rise or exceed 50 and bearish strategies when readings fall. The passage discusses backtests using PMI readings for S&P 500 and gold. One S&P 500 strategy invested when readings were above 50, was invested 72% of the time, returned 7.3% annually versus 8.5% for the S&P 500, and reduced drawdowns. The author concludes the ISM Manufacturing Index is not a particularly good contrarian indicator, likely because it is lagging and already discounted by markets.

The PMI includes seasonal adjustments to account for recurring factors such as weather, holidays, and seasonal demand. The passage states both that factors may be weighted by relative importance using statistical analysis and that the PMI gives equal weight to new orders, production, employment, supplier deliveries, and inventories. Data can be downloaded from ISM’s homepage, and the passage mentions a Google Sheet with data back to 1970.

The passage presents SQuID, “Survey and Questionnaire Item Embeddings Differentials,” a method for using semantic embeddings of questionnaire items in psychometric analysis. The authors argue that NLP can help address the cost and data-quality challenges of collecting large human-rating samples for questionnaire development.

Prior embedding-based psychometric approaches showed promise but struggled to reproduce negative correlations between items, which are important in many questionnaires. SQuID addresses this by subtracting the average questionnaire embedding from each item embedding, reducing shared linguistic features and enabling negative correlations without domain-specific fine-tuning.

The authors test the method on the Revised Portrait Value Questionnaire (PVQ-RR), a 57-item survey measuring 19 value dimensions in Schwartz’s theory of basic human values. They compare embeddings from several models with human rater data. Linq-Embed-Mistral performs best, showing internal consistency comparable to or above human data on average. Dimension-level similarities from embeddings correlate substantially with those from human ratings, and multidimensional scaling recovers a circular value structure similar to the theory-based human configuration. Procrustes transformation shows fair similarity between embedding-derived and human-derived configurations.

The authors conclude that semantic embeddings, when processed with SQuID, can complement human judgments in psychometric workflows while remaining flexible, cheap, and scalable. They emphasize that embeddings should not replace human participants, note unresolved validity and methodological questions, and discuss potential ethical concerns, including effects on crowdworkers and risks of treating LLM-derived patterns as normative standards.

The paper describes the Shayona team’s participation in SMM4H 2023 Task-1 and Task-4, both binary classification tasks using social media data. Task-1 focused on identifying tweets that self-report COVID-19 diagnosis, while Task-4 focused on identifying social anxiety disorder diagnosis reports from r/socialanxiety data.

For Task-1, the dataset included 7,600 training tweets, 400 validation tweets, and 10,000 test tweets. For Task-4, it included 6,090 training entries, 680 validation entries, and 1,347 test entries. Preprocessing removed non-alphabet characters, tags, emojis, URLs, stopwords, and punctuation.

The authors tested RoBERTa, fine-tuned BERT, and a hybrid BERT+LightGBM model. They used the Hugging Face model “digitalepidemiologylab/covid-twitter-bert-v2,” fine-tuned it, extracted hidden [CLS] tokens from the last three BERT layers, and trained LightGBM with Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization. On Task-1 validation data, RoBERTa scored 0.83 F1, BERT scored 0.89, and BERT+LightGBM scored 0.93. On Task-1 test data, BERT+LightGBM achieved precision 0.949, recall 0.938, and F1 0.943. The same hybrid architecture was used for Task-4, achieving precision 0.756, recall 0.871, and F1 0.809.

The authors conclude that combining BERT embeddings with LightGBM performed best for Task-1 and suggest Task-4 could improve with a BERT model pretrained on task-relevant data.

The passage describes NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU architecture features for AI, HPC, and data center workloads. A100 supports fine-grained 2:4 structured sparsity, pruning trained weights so two of every four values are non-zero, compressing weights for a 2x reduction in data footprint and bandwidth. Sparse Tensor Core MMA instructions skip zero values, doubling Tensor Core compute throughput with virtually no inferencing accuracy loss across evaluated networks after fine-tuning.

A100 includes a combined L1 data cache and shared memory subsystem with 192 KB per SM, compared with 128 KB in V100, and supports simultaneous FP32 and INT32 execution. Its memory system includes 40 GB of HBM2 delivering 1555 GB/sec bandwidth, SECDED ECC protection, and a 40 MB L2 cache, 6.7x larger than V100, with 2.3x higher L2 bandwidth. Compute Data Compression can improve DRAM and L2 bandwidth by up to 4x and L2 capacity by up to 2x.

A100 improves Tensor Core performance through third-generation Tensor Cores, more SMs than V100, larger tensor operations, improved data sharing, fewer register accesses, asynchronous copy instructions, asynchronous barriers, larger shared memory allocation, higher HBM2 and L2 bandwidth, and L2 cache residency controls. CUDA 11 supports A100 features including Tensor Cores, sparsity, CUDA Graphs, Multi-Instance GPU, asynchronous copy, asynchronous barriers, L2 residency controls, and Cooperative Groups improvements.

Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) can partition one A100 into up to seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated SMs, L2 cache banks, memory controllers, DRAM paths, and frame buffer memory. MIG supports predictable throughput, latency, QoS, fault isolation, multi-tenant and single-tenant use cases, virtual machines, containers, and migration of vGPUs between GPU Instances or GPUs. Compute Instances within GPU Instances allow multiple contexts to execute independently.

A100 implements third-generation NVLink with twelve links, 600 GB/sec total bandwidth, improved error detection and recovery, and support for peer GPU memory access. It also supports PCIe Gen 4 at 31.5 GB/sec per direction for x16 connections and SR-IOV virtualization. Additional features include improved fault detection and containment, NVJPG hardware JPEG decode, an Optical Flow Accelerator, faster FP16 and FP32 atomics than V100, and five NVDEC units.

DGX A100 uses eight A100 GPUs connected with NVLink and NVSwitch, delivering up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance, up to 56 isolated GPU Instances through MIG, and support for scaling through Mellanox HDR InfiniBand, Magnum IO, NGC containers, and DGX software. The appendix explains sparsity, pruning, fine-grained and coarse-grained sparsity, and how A100’s structured sparsity aims to preserve balanced workloads and accuracy while improving compute and memory efficiency.

The passage describes NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU architecture and its improvements over Tesla V100. A100 SMs include four redesigned Tensor Cores, each capable of 256 FP16 FMA operations per clock, delivering 1024 FP16 FMAs per SM per clock. Across 108 SMs and 432 Tensor Cores, A100 provides up to 312 TFLOPS of dense mixed-precision FP16/FP32 performance, 2.5x V100 Tensor Core performance.

A100 Tensor Cores support FP16, INT8, INT4, binary, TF32, BF16, and FP64 formats. TF32 enables tensor-core acceleration for AI training using FP32 inputs and outputs with no script changes, while FP16 or BF16 mixed precision offers higher throughput. A100 also accelerates HPC workloads with FP64 Tensor Cores, delivering 19.5 TFLOPS peak FP64 throughput, 2.5x Tesla V100. In cuSOLVER TCAIRS tests, TF32 showed the fastest and most robust mixed-precision iterative refinement results, with a 2.0x geomean speedup over an FP64 solver.

A100 introduces fine-grained structured sparsity using a 2:4 sparse pattern, allowing Tensor Cores to skip zero values and double compute throughput. NVIDIA describes a pruning and fine-tuning workflow that achieves virtually no inference accuracy loss across evaluated networks.

The architecture includes a combined L1 cache/shared memory subsystem with 192 KB per SM, separate FP32 and INT32 cores for simultaneous execution, 40 GB HBM2 memory with 1555 GB/sec bandwidth, SECDED ECC protection, and a 40 MB L2 cache, 6.7x larger than V100. L2 bandwidth is 2.3x higher than V100, and Compute Data Compression can improve DRAM bandwidth, L2 bandwidth, and L2 capacity.

A100 improves Tensor Core efficiency with broader warp-level data sharing, fewer issued instructions, fewer register accesses, asynchronous global-to-shared memory copy, asynchronous barriers, larger shared memory allocation, cache residency controls, and compression. CUDA 11 supports these features along with Tensor Cores, sparsity, CUDA Graphs, MIG, and L2 controls.

Multi-Instance GPU allows one A100 to be partitioned into up to seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated SMs, L2 cache slices, memory controllers, and DRAM bandwidth. MIG supports QoS, fault isolation, multi-tenant use, virtual machines, containers, and migration of vGPUs between compatible GPU Instances. Compute Instances further subdivide GPU Instances and support MPS.

A100 includes third-generation NVLink with twelve links and 600 GB/sec total bandwidth, PCIe Gen 4 with 31.5 GB/sec per direction for x16 connections, and SR-IOV. It adds improved error detection, isolation, containment, and recovery, especially for MIG and NVLink-connected systems.

Additional features include hardware JPEG decoding through NVJPG, an Optical Flow Accelerator, improved FP16 and FP32 atomic throughput, and five NVDEC units. DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs, six NVSwitches, third-generation NVLink, Mellanox ConnectX-6 HDR InfiniBand, and software from NGC, delivering up to 5 PFLOPS and up to 56 isolated GPU Instances through MIG.

The ADS868xW device provides an internal 4.096V reference selected by setting INTREF_DIS to 0; REFIO becomes an output and requires at least a 4.7µF capacitor to REFGND. REFIO must not drive external loads unless buffered. The internal reference is factory-trimmed, temperature compensated from –40°C to +125°C, and can shift after solder reflow due to thermal stress. For external reference mode, INTREF_DIS is set to 1 and a 4.096V reference is applied to REFIO; the internal buffer drives REFCAP, which requires at least 10µF plus a 1µF high-frequency decoupling capacitor.

The ADC supports single-ended and differential bipolar or unipolar input ranges and outputs straight-binary data. It includes alarm functions on the ALARM/SDO-1/GPO pin when configured: an input alarm with programmable high and low thresholds and hysteresis, and an AVDD alarm with fixed typical thresholds of 4.7V and 5.3V. Alarm status is available through the output pin, ALARM_REG, or appended output flags. Active flags clear after conversion if the condition ends, while tripped flags clear when ALARM_REG is read.

The multiSPI interface supports standard SPI, dual-SDO, source-synchronous modes, and daisy-chain operation. The device has RESET, ACQ, and CONV states controlled by RST and CONVST/CS. RESET can be configured as application reset or power-on reset. ACQ acquires the input signal, and CONV begins on a CONVST/CS rising edge and completes using an internal clock.

Programming uses nine configuration registers and 32-bit data transfer frames. Frames begin on CONVST/CS falling edge and end on the following rising edge. A 32-clock frame is optimal; shorter frames invalidate writes but can read MSBs, while longer frames use the last 32 bits as the command. Supported commands include register reads, writes, set, clear, and half-word operations. Output data can include conversion results, register data, fixed patterns, device address, range flags, alarm flags, and parity.

The register map includes DEVICE_ID_REG, RST_PWRCTL_REG, SDI_CTL_REG, SDO_CTL_REG, DATAOUT_CTL_REG, RANGE_SEL_REG, ALARM_REG, ALARM_H_TH_REG, and ALARM_L_TH_REG. The application example combines ADS8681W with an eight-channel MUX36D08 for an industrial analog input module supporting standard voltage and current inputs. The device includes programmable gain, ADC driver, reference, overvoltage protection, input alarm, and AVDD alarm.

Power supplies AVDD and DVDD are separate and should be decoupled with capacitors. Low-power NAP and power-down modes reduce consumption at lower throughput rates. Layout guidance recommends separating analog and digital sections, keeping supplies well bypassed, placing reference capacitors close to device pins, and decoupling REFIO when using the internal reference.

The Rate of Change (ROC or PROC) is a momentum-based technical indicator that compares a security’s current price with its price “n” periods ago and plots the result as an oscillator around a zero line. Positive values indicate upward momentum, while negative values indicate downward momentum. Traders use ROC to assess momentum, identify overbought or oversold conditions, track centerline crossovers, and spot bullish or bearish divergences that may signal reversals.

The ROC period depends on trading style: shorter periods are more sensitive and produce more signals, while longer periods are smoother but slower. ROC can be applied across markets with real-time price data, but it is prone to whipsaws in volatile markets and may perform better when used with trend direction and other indicators such as moving averages or trendlines. The passage emphasizes backtesting, optimization, and robustness before using ROC strategies.

Backtested ROC strategies discussed include oversold mean reversion, breakouts, zero-line crosses, and divergences. The oversold strategy showed some promise but had sharp setbacks, while breakout and zero-line crossover tests performed poorly. The passage concludes that ROC strategies are generally inferior to indicators such as RSI, stochastic, and Williams %R.

AMD Geode CS5535 Companion Device Silicon Revision A3 specification update lists multiple hardware issues, impacts, and workarounds. Illegal LBAR values at 10000h or higher can be set but have no operational impact and should not be used. Several clock-gating issues can cause missed PIC interrupts, lost GLIU statistics-counter ASMIs, UART CEIR failure, and unreliable USB controller register reads; affected clock gating should be disabled. ATAC and ACC PRD prefetch behavior can expose errors with unaligned PRD tables or on-the-fly PRD changes; PRD tables should be defined in advance or updated safely. UDMA write CRC errors may occur after certain UDMA read host terminations; ATAC UDMA I/O blocking should be used. IDE/ATAPI failures can occur if bus mastering is enabled before PIO command packets; normal UDMA sequencing is required.

ACPI/PMC registers have access-size limitations: byte accesses to PM1_EN and PM1_STS can hang, and WORD/BYTE writes may corrupt PMC registers; SMI traps or DWORD access are recommended. KEL has several emulation and snoop-mode register-state issues requiring software workarounds. Other noted issues include unsupported PIC polling mode, unreliable SSMI generation when IRQs coincide, RTC CMOS read anomalies, LPC I/O failures during block/demand DMA, LPC aborts with some LPC-to-ISA bridges, SMB NEGACK and hold-time problems, GPIO high-bank atomic write failures after suspend, missing LOWBAT_FLAG after abnormal standby, and sleep-exit delay programming requirements. Some issues are described as having no expected real-world impact or no required resolution.
