The passage describes SD Memory Card initialization, identification, data transfer, protection, and command behavior.

After bus activation, the host initializes cards using ACMD41, setting operational conditions and the HCS bit to indicate SDHC/SDXC support. CMD8 expands ACMD41 behavior and should be issued before ACMD41 for cards compliant with Version 2.00 or later. The OCR busy bit indicates initialization progress, which must complete within 1 second; the host repeats ACMD41 until ready or timeout. CCS in the ACMD41 response identifies SDSC versus SDHC/SDXC when valid. The host then uses CMD2 to obtain each card’s CID and CMD3 to assign an RCA, moving cards to Stand-by State. SDXC initialization is identical to SDHC, with user capacity specified by C_SIZE and at least 32GB.

ACMD41 argument rules distinguish inquiry CMD41, first ACMD41, and repeated ACMD41. XPC selects SDXC power operation, while S18R requests 1.8V signaling for UHS-I. If allowed, the card returns S18A=1 and the host issues CMD11 for voltage switching. UHS-I initialization includes voltage switching, checking lock status, optional CMD42 unlock, driver strength selection via CMD6, UHS-I mode selection, and tuning with CMD19 where required.

In Data Transfer Mode, the host may switch from fOD to fPP, read CSD with CMD9, optionally configure DSR with CMD4, and select a single card using CMD7. Data transfers are point-to-point with the selected card. Read and write commands can be aborted with CMD12. Write operations may enter Programming State, hold DAT0 low as busy, and may continue when another card is selected. Resetting a card with CMD0 or CMD15 terminates active programming and may destroy data.

Bus width defaults to 1-bit and may be changed with ACMD6 only when allowed; locked cards reject ACMD6. Reads and writes are block-oriented, CRC-protected, and use CMD17/CMD18 for reads and CMD24/CMD25 and related commands for writes. SDHC and SDXC use fixed 512-byte block addressing for memory access, while SDSC uses byte addressing and CMD16-defined block length. Partial and misaligned accesses are restricted depending on card capability.

Erase uses CMD32, CMD33, and CMD38 in sequence. DISCARD and FULE are CMD38 variants for SDHC/SDXC only and are unsupported through SPI. DISCARD treats affected contents as “don’t care,” while FULE logically erases the full user area. Both require support bits in SD_STATUS, have defined busy behavior, and reset their sequence on errors.

Write protection includes mechanical switch handling by the host, optional internal card protection, and password-based card lock. CMD42 manages password setting, clearing, locking, unlocking, force erase, and Card Ownership Protection (COP). Passwords are stored in non-volatile PWD/PWD_LEN registers. Locked cards accept only specified basic, initialization, status, and lock-related commands and do not allow data access. COP adds FEP management, COP Unlock, FEP Force Erase, and restrictions that disable Force Erase and PWD clearing while FEP is set.

APP_CMD (CMD55) causes the next command to be interpreted as an application-specific command when defined. CMD6 switches or checks card functions, including bus speed, command system, UHS-I driver strength, and power limit. CMD6 supports mode 0 for checking support and consumption and mode 1 for switching functions, returning a 512-bit status block. High-Speed mode is optional and entered using CMD6 on Version 1.10 or later cards. Command system switching affects reserved commands CMD34–37, CMD50, and CMD57.

The mother appealed a judgment denying her custody of her son Edward and confirming custody in the father. The ADS868xW supports single-ended and differential inputs with bipolar and unipolar ranges, outputting straight-binary ADC data. Its LSB size equals FSR/2^16, with values listed for VREF = 4.096 V.

The device provides alarm functions through the ALARM/SDO-1/GPO pin when configured. Input alarms compare ADC input values against programmable high and low thresholds with programmable hysteresis. AVDD alarms monitor fixed typical thresholds of 4.7 V and 5.3 V. Alarm flags include active and tripped flags, readable through ALARM_REG, the ALARM pin, or appended output data.

Communication uses a multiSPI digital interface with input/output shift registers, configuration registers, and protocol control. The device supports single-device standard SPI, full multiSPI options, and daisy-chain topologies. In daisy-chain mode, devices share CONVST/CS and SCLK, shift data through SDO-0 to SDI, and require optimal frames of 32 × N SCLK capture edges for N devices.

The device operates in RESET, ACQ, and CONV states controlled by RST and CONVST/CS. RESET can be application reset or power-on reset. ACQ acquires the analog input, while CONV begins on a CONVST/CS rising edge and uses an internal clock until conversion completes.

Programming uses nine configuration registers and supports read and write transfers. A data frame begins on the falling edge of CONVST/CS and ends on the next rising edge. Frames with 32 SCLKs are optimal; shorter frames invalidate writes but can read MSBs, while longer frames use the last 32 input bits as the command. Output data may contain conversion results, register data, fixed patterns, device address, range flags, alarm flags, and parity.

The multiSPI interface supports standard SPI protocols for configuration and readout, dual-SDO output, and source-synchronous read protocols using RVS as an output clock. Configuration registers control device ID, reset and power, SDI/SDO modes, output formatting, input range, alarms, and alarm thresholds.

Application information describes using ADS8681W with an MUX36D08 for an eight-channel industrial analog input module supporting voltage and current inputs. The device integrates a programmable gain amplifier, ADC driver, reference, overvoltage protection, input alarm, and AVDD alarm. Power recommendations include separate AVDD and DVDD supplies, decoupling capacitors, NAP mode, and power-down mode. Layout guidance recommends separating analog and digital sections and placing supply and reference capacitors close to device pins.

The passage examines digital storytelling in African higher education and teacher training. It presents digital storytelling as a multimedia approach that combines text, images, audio, video, and narration to support learning, identity expression, creativity, collaboration, digital literacy, critical thinking, problem-solving, and reflective practice. The study uses qualitative document analysis of 15 African-context research articles selected from academic databases using criteria related to education, higher education, social sciences, and digital storytelling.

Findings show that digital storytelling has been used in contexts including pre-service teacher education, geography education, oral language development, postgraduate research, cultural preservation, and work with marginalized groups. Reported benefits include increased student engagement, improved map-reading and oral performance, stronger peer learning, community building, cultural understanding, self-expression, motivation, and higher-order thinking. It also supports the preservation and modernization of oral traditions and indigenous knowledge.

The passage also identifies challenges to implementation, including limited resources, inconsistent electricity, inadequate digital equipment, low technological confidence or competence, rigid curricula, and time constraints. It concludes that digital storytelling is adaptable across educational settings in Africa and can promote empowerment, cultural enrichment, and transformative learning when the emphasis remains on narrative content rather than technology alone.

William Green introduces ordinary differential equation initial value problems (ODE-IVPs), defining ODEs as involving derivatives with respect to one variable and IVPs as problems where all initial conditions are specified at one value of that variable. He explains how higher-order equations can be rewritten as first-order systems in standard form for numerical solvers, including Matlab’s expected \(f(t,y)\) format.

The lecture describes expected ODE solver outputs: time points and corresponding solution vectors, often for plotting or final-value extraction. Green presents the Forward Euler method from a truncated Taylor expansion and compares it to the rectangle rule, noting its first-order error scaling and poor efficiency for improving accuracy. He contrasts this with trapezoid and midpoint rules, which use better estimates of the average derivative and improve error scaling.

He explains that for ODEs where \(f\) depends on \(y\), future values of \(y\) are unknown, making direct use of midpoint or trapezoid formulas harder. Runge-Kutta methods address this by estimating intermediate values, such as second-order Runge-Kutta using a Forward Euler estimate at the midpoint. Matlab’s ODE45 is described as using fourth- and fifth-order Runge-Kutta formulas to estimate error and choose step sizes.

The lecture then focuses on error propagation and numerical stability. Errors from each step can be amplified depending on the norm of a matrix involving the update formula’s Jacobian. Stable methods reduce earlier errors, while unstable ones amplify them. Green notes that systems with positive Jacobian eigenvalues are intrinsically unstable, but even stable physical systems can become numerically unstable with poor methods or large time steps. A scalar example, \(dy/dt=-2y\), shows Forward Euler producing oscillations or blow-up for too-large step sizes instead of the true decaying solution. The lecture ends by noting that homework will involve writing ODE solvers and that implicit solvers will be discussed next.

The chapter addresses representation and validation of digital business processes in extended enterprises, where organizations collaborate across boundaries. It adopts an MDA-driven business process model with three components: a static domain model describing entities, a workflow model specifying activities, and a value model describing exchanges between parties.

For static modeling, the chapter discusses business rules expressed in controlled natural languages such as ACE and SBVR. These can be translated into logic-based representations for automated reasoning, but challenges arise because different entities may require different assumptions. Closed-world reasoning suits complete, controlled data, while open-world reasoning is needed for incomplete or externally sourced knowledge common in inter-organizational settings. OWL/DL can represent incomplete knowledge but has limited expressiveness, while Horn rules and SWRL can express some rules but may lose semantics when combined with open-world constructs. Modal interpretations of business rules are also needed, distinguishing alethic rules, which cannot be violated, from deontic rules, which express obligations that may be violated.

For workflow modeling, the chapter reviews graphical process-flow languages such as BPMN and UML Activity Diagrams. Dynamic process behavior is often modeled using Petri nets, π-calculus, situation calculus, or temporal logic. Declarative representations have limits for dynamic and concurrent systems but support consistency checking, data export, and annotation. A BPMN example shows how process elements can be represented as assertions and checked against static model requirements.

For value modeling, the chapter presents graphical and logic-based approaches. Using an example involving manufacturers, distributors, retailers, web-enabled retailers, logistics providers, and customers, it shows how value transfers and dependencies can be modeled to estimate profitability. Graphical e3-value models and logic-based Prolog-style representations both describe actors, exchanges, dependencies, and quantified estimates.

The chapter then examines relations between the static, workflow, and value models. Since different models represent different aspects, equivalence is generally unsuitable, while consistency checking is appropriate. Static consistency checks whether value exchanges correspond to business objects exchanged in process models. Semi-dynamic consistency checks whether value-model forecasts can be achieved by the process-flow model. Dynamic consistency compares runtime behavior, through log files, with value-model expectations and process-flow implementations. Process mining can derive process models from log data.

The conclusion states that business process models increasingly require multi-faceted representations supporting workflow, organizational structure, value chains, and actor positions. The chapter emphasizes logic-based models beneath visual representations and argues for hybrid reasoning combining Semantic Web-style inference with Prolog-like reasoning. Open issues include detecting critical areas when models fail and representing the pragmatic reasons behind stakeholder actions.

Court documents say Steve Wynn settled in 2006 with a second woman who accused him of sexual misconduct and recently reported her to the FBI for alleged extortion. The lecture introduces AMO physics as a field defined by its community, its building blocks—atoms, molecules, photons, and electromagnetic fields—and its focus on low-energy quantum systems. Historically centered on individual particles and collisions in gases, AMO physics has expanded into few-body and many-body physics, entanglement, quantum information, quantum gases, and areas overlapping with condensed matter physics, especially when systems are controlled optically.

The professor describes the field’s evolution from observing nature to controlling it. Key advances include optical pumping for internal-state control, laser cooling and Bose-Einstein condensation for motional control, and control of single atoms and photons. Future directions are framed as using precise control of simple quantum building blocks to create complex entangled and many-body states.

Technological developments driving the field include lasers, diode and solid-state lasers, ultrashort and high-intensity pulses, frequency combs, and high-finesse cavities. The lecture also reviews changing paradigms in AMO physics, from atomic structure and optical pumping to laser spectroscopy, magneto-optical traps, Bose-Einstein condensation, ultracold fermions, entanglement, and possible future breakthroughs in quantum computation, topological states, and micromechanical oscillators.

The course will cover light-atom interactions from first principles, QED, stimulated and spontaneous emission, open quantum systems, density matrices, master equations, mechanical forces of light, trapping and cooling, photon quantum properties, quantum information concepts, and many-body physics of quantum gases. It will not focus on high-energy physics, high-energy collisions, advanced atomic structure, or high-intensity short-pulse laser physics. Requirements include problem sets and a term paper, with no midterm or final.

As an introductory example, the professor discusses atoms in optical lattices. Standing waves of light create periodic potentials for atoms, which can be analyzed through classical potentials, photon pictures, and microscopic forces. Depending on conditions, optical lattices can produce Sisyphus cooling, precision atomic clocks using deep lattices and magic wavelengths, tunneling and many-body effects in shallow lattices, Mott insulators, band-structure physics, atom interferometry, and measurements of dynamic structure factors in interacting systems. The example illustrates how AMO tools can serve both precision measurement and many-body physics.

University of Utah scientists mapped the near-surface geology around Yellowstone’s Old Faithful using a dense temporary network of 133 small portable seismometers and new seismic analysis techniques. The study identified a hydrothermal reservoir feeding the geyser and examined ground tremors between eruptions. Researchers found that tremors build as the reservoir refills with hot water and pressurized bubbles collapse, with eruptions occurring at the end of the shaking. Seismic data suggest the reservoir is a network of cracks and fractures about 200 meters wide, holding roughly 300,000 cubic meters of water, while each eruption releases about 30 cubic meters. The team plans further surveys to study temperature effects, earthquake wave behavior, and other geyser basins.

Secretary Stettinius urged governments to approach a general conference flexibly and avoid formal commitments, noting the Dumbarton Oaks proposals were informal and might need modification. Discussions addressed objections to the name “United Nations” and possible enumeration of principles. In January 1945, Stettinius prepared for Yalta and Mexico City, pressed Latin American “associated nations” to qualify for the United Nations Conference by declaring war, and directed staff to prepare policy memoranda. He sought readiness to call the conference, settle delegation details, and address unresolved voting procedures, including Security Council unanimity and British acceptance of a compromise formula.

France named 18 initial recipients of President Emmanuel Macron’s “Make Our Planet Great Again” climate grants, including 13 based in the U.S. U.S.-based scientists Camille Parmesan and Benjamin Sanderson said the all-expenses-paid opportunity would let them continue climate research in Europe amid concerns about funding and support under President Donald Trump. Parmesan will work at an experimental ecology station in the Pyrenees, while Sanderson will live in Toulouse, where France’s national meteorological service is based.

The First Circuit affirmed the denial of Ronald L. Johnson’s habeas corpus petition challenging the admission of his confession from a 1964 Massachusetts murder and robbery trial. Johnson argued that the trial court failed to consider the totality of the circumstances, that the state bore the burden of proving voluntariness under Lego v. Twomey, and that his confession was involuntary as a matter of law.

The court found it unnecessary to decide the first two issues because it independently reviewed the undisputed facts under the totality-of-the-circumstances standard. Johnson had been arrested after a police chase and crash, was injured, had limited education and an I.Q. of 86, was not given Miranda warnings, went through several lineups, and confessed after about forty minutes of questioning roughly eight and one-half hours after arrest.

The court concluded that these circumstances did not show his will was overborne. It emphasized Johnson’s prior experience with police and courts, his hostile and resistant conduct toward police, his challenges to lineup witnesses, the absence of credited evidence that police beat or threatened him, and evidence that he appeared alert during questioning. His injuries, lack of sleep, limited food, and confrontation with incriminating identifications did not render the confession involuntary. The confession was held voluntary, and the district court’s judgment was affirmed.

The Healthy Davis/Yolo Together program provided free COVID-19 testing in Davis and Yolo County from November 2020 to June 2022. This study describes testing participation, participant demographics, changes over pandemic variant periods, and frequent testing patterns. The analysis included 770,165 tests among 89,924 Yolo County residents, reaching about 41.1% of Yolo County and 78.4% of Davis residents. Most tests were saliva PCR tests.

Testing peaked during the Omicron period, with the highest daily testing rate, highest number of positive cases, and highest share of frequent testers. Overall, 12,626 tests were positive among 11,545 individuals. Participation was generally steady across demographic groups, though women, people aged 19–44, and White participants were consistently the most frequent testers. Higher positivity rates were observed among American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander, Latino participants, and adults aged 20–44.

The program retained participants and enrolled new testers over time, but participation declined after Omicron. The authors note that testing behavior may have been influenced by changing risk perception, pandemic fatigue, testing requirements, vaccines, at-home tests, misinformation, and trust, though the data do not allow conclusions about causes. The study suggests large-scale testing data can inform future public health strategies, while emphasizing the need for additional behavioral data to better understand uptake of preventive measures.

Worcester paid more than $11 million in overtime in 2017, including over $7 million to police, fire and public works employees. Police employees received $4.4 million in overtime and $9.3 million in detail pay, with some officers earning more from details than regular salary. Officials said overtime was driven by training, special events, grants, emergencies and investigations, not understaffing. The city had 7,287 payroll employees, 223 earning over $100,000 in regular pay, and City Manager Edward Augustus Jr. was the highest paid.

Indiana flu season can last until mid-April, with 278 flu deaths reported this season by the Indiana State Department of Health. IU Health officials said pathogens such as flu and norovirus can survive on surfaces and spread when people touch contaminated objects and then their faces. In an IU Health lab experiment, FOX59’s Olivia McClellan’s hands showed 15 types of bacteria before and after handwashing, with little difference, suggesting she needed to scrub longer and harder. Her cellphone tested positive for 10 types of bacteria consistent with normal mouth, throat and skin flora. IU Health recommends washing hands with soap for 20–30 seconds, scrubbing all areas including under fingernails, and rinsing thoroughly, especially after bathroom use, diaper changes, caring for sick people, and before eating.

India’s Supreme Court ordered that parties cannot seek votes in the name of religion, caste, creed, community or language. The author argues the order is problematic because identity-based mobilisation has helped marginalised communities challenge historic discrimination and gain political representation. The piece says communal appeals and hate politics should be addressed through existing laws, stronger rule of law and democratic political contestation, not judicial fiat. It also argues the order is difficult to implement because caste, religion and language influence elections at all levels, and that Indian electoral democracy should be allowed to evolve without artificial bans.

The study examines how walking, as an everyday bodily and sensory practice, can become an aesthetic experience through art-based practices in fine arts teacher education. It frames walking as an interaction between self, body, place, society, and perception, drawing on place-based education, critical art education, aesthetic inquiry, and Dewey’s view that everyday practices and aesthetic experiences can enrich one another.

Conducted over 10 weeks in 2023 in an undergraduate fine arts teaching program at a university in western Türkiye, the study involved seven prospective teachers. Because classes were online after the 2023 Türkiye earthquake, participants integrated walking into their daily routines in natural areas, city centers, neighborhoods, squares, parks, and coastal settings. Data included visual diaries, course recordings, participant texts, artworks, and interviews. The researchers used an art-based, phenomenological, interpretive methodology and thematic analysis with triangulation and participant validation.

The course process began with participants writing about walking, then creating visual diaries and texts based on walking experiences. They examined walking-related artworks, especially Francis Alÿs’ “The Collector,” and used aesthetic inquiry to analyze walking, place, sound, objects, and social meaning. Participants then took photographs during walks, questioned their images, and developed artworks or designs using media such as performance, video, collage, and digital art.

Findings showed that participants’ initial descriptions of walking as ordinary physical movement expanded into broader meanings such as freedom, making a living, finding oneself, death, dreaming, and social critique. Through repeated walks, visual diaries, photography, and artistic inquiry, they became more attentive to sounds, animals, people, urban rhythms, pollution, obstacles, loneliness, belonging, and social problems. Their works reflected both personal and social concerns, including street sounds, urban life, environmental awareness, accessibility, and the relationship between daily life and art.

Participants reported that walking helped them connect art, life, and pedagogy, develop multiple perspectives, and consider everyday practices as course content. Some struggled with visualizing experiences, choosing subjects, performing in public, or producing satisfying artworks. The study concludes that walking can support prospective teachers in developing aesthetic awareness, environmental and social sensitivity, and art-based approaches that connect lived experience with teaching.

Abraaj, a private equity firm focused on developing economies, promoted its $1 billion health care fund as a way to earn strong returns while improving hospitals in Nigeria, Pakistan and India. The fund had also struggled, including weaker-than-expected results from its CARE hospital investment in India.

The passage discusses the impact of the #MeToo movement on Canadian politics following resignations by Jamie Baillie, Patrick Brown, and Kent Hehr amid misconduct allegations. It notes backlash over due process and comparisons to McCarthyism, while arguing that political parties may hold leaders to higher standards when allegations undermine their ability to serve. Indiana plans to use outcomes-based contracts with private tutoring providers to improve middle school reading, tying pay partly to student gains. State officials say no proven model exists to copy, but vendors have offered solutions after scores fell. Similar pay-for-performance efforts in states and districts including Texas, Florida, Arkansas and Denver have had mixed results, with limited research and concerns about attendance, scheduling and measurement. The Center for Outcomes-Based Contracting recommends at least 40% of pay depend on student outcomes and reports about half of 2025 contract goals were met. Indiana has not finalized contract details and is seeking funding, but officials say payment should depend on measurable improvements for struggling readers.
